blocks.html: Microeconomics zoomed in on one market at a time. Macroeconomics steps back to look at the whole economy. A good first picture is the circular flow. It builds on the factors of production (land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship) and on how a market economy answers the basic questions.

Households and firms meet in two markets. In the product market, households buy goods and services from firms. In the factor (resource) market, households sell the use of their labor, land and capital to firms. Money flows one way around the loop; goods, services and resources flow the other way.

Every purchase has two sides. When you pay a bakery \$5 for bread, that \$5 is your spending and the bakery's revenue. The bakery then pays it out as wages, rent, interest and profit, which are the incomes of households. So one person's spending is another person's income. That is why we can measure the size of an economy either by adding up spending or by adding up income: they are the same dollars counted at two points on the loop.

blocks.name: ec-circularflow
blocks.cap: The simple circular flow. Press "Follow a dollar" to watch one dollar of spending become revenue, then income, then spending again. The toggles add government, financial markets and the rest of the world.

blocks.html: Real economies have more sectors. Households also pay taxes, save, and buy imports. Each of these is a leakage: money that leaves the loop of spending on our own output. Firms' investment, government purchases and exports are injections: spending that enters the loop from outside households. When injections are larger than leakages, total spending tends to grow; when leakages are larger, it tends to shrink.

blocks.title: Which way does each flow go?
blocks.q: Maria works at a bike shop and earns \$600 a week. On Saturday she spends \$80 at a grocery store. Describe each flow.
steps: Her work is a resource (labor). She sells it in the factor market, so labor flows from a household to a firm.
The \$600 is income. It flows from the firm to the household in the factor market.
The groceries are products. They flow from the store (a firm) to Maria in the product market.
The \$80 is spending. It flows from Maria to the store in the product market, where it becomes the store's revenue.
blocks.a: Labor and groceries move one way; the \$600 wage and the \$80 payment move the other way.

blocks.html: Putting households on the selling side of the product market, or thinking money disappears when it is spent. Households buy products and sell resources; firms do the reverse. And spent money does not vanish: it becomes a firm's revenue and then someone's income. Quick check: for any arrow, ask "who receives this?" Someone always does.

blocks.html: The The Circular Flow showed that the economy's spending and income go around a loop. To measure how much an economy produces, economists count the spending on its output in a careful way. The result is gross domestic product, or GDP.
GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, usually a quarter or a year.

Each word in the definition keeps GDP from counting something twice or counting something that was not made. Market value means we add things up by their prices, so cars and haircuts can be combined in dollars. Final goods are sold to their last user; the flour inside a loaf of bread is already in the bread's price, so counting the flour too would double-count it. Produced in the period leaves out used goods, which were counted the year they were made. Within a country means location, not ownership: a Japanese-owned car plant in Kentucky adds to U.S. GDP.

items: Counted: new goods and services sold to households, businesses, government and foreigners; new homes; goods produced this year but still unsold (they count as additions to inventories).

Not counted: intermediate goods (already inside the final price), used goods, purchases of stocks and bonds (a change of ownership, not production), transfer payments such as Social Security checks (nothing is produced in return), and unpaid work at home.

blocks.html: GDP is the market value of final output (What GDP Counts). One way to add it up is to ask who bought that output. Every final buyer falls into one of four groups.

$$GDP = C + I + G + NX$$ Consumption ($C$) is household spending on goods and services. Investment ($I$) is spending on new capital goods, new homes and additions to inventories. Government purchases ($G$) are goods and services bought by all levels of government. Net exports are exports minus imports: $NX = X - M$.

Why subtract imports? Not because imports "shrink" the economy. When a family buys a \$600 phone made abroad, that \$600 is already inside $C$. It was not produced here, so GDP must take it back out. Subtracting $M$ removes foreign production that was counted in $C$, $I$ or $G$. Exports are added because they are made here but bought by foreigners, so they appear in none of the other three.

blocks.html: GDP counts only final goods. But most products pass through several firms on the way to you. Value added gives a second way to measure GDP that never double-counts, and it shows why the income approach gives the same total.

A firm's value added is the value of what it sells minus what it paid other firms for inputs. Adding the value added at every stage of production gives the price of the final good, so the sum of value added across the economy equals GDP.

Follow a loaf of bread. A farmer grows wheat and sells it to a miller for \$0.30. The miller grinds it and sells flour to a baker for \$0.50, adding \$0.20. The baker sells the bread to a grocer for \$0.80, adding \$0.30, and the grocer sells it to you for \$1.00, adding \$0.20. The value added sums to $0.30 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.20 = 1.00$, the final price. Adding all four sales instead gives \$2.60, which counts the wheat four times. And each stage's value added is paid out as wages, rent, interest and profit, so it is also the income earned at that stage. That is why measuring GDP by spending, by value added, or by income gives the same total.

blocks.html: Total GDP tells you how much an economy produces (GDP = C + I + G + NX). To compare living standards, divide by the number of people. With GDP in trillions and population in millions, scientific notation keeps the powers of ten straight.

$$\text{GDP per person} = \dfrac{\text{GDP}}{\text{population}}$$ It is the most common single measure of average living standards. But GDP leaves out some things that matter for well-being, so it is a useful measure, not a complete one.

A country with many people can have a huge total GDP even if each person produces little, and a small country can have a modest total with high output per person. Dividing by population puts countries of different sizes on the same footing. As a growth rate, GDP per person grows by about the growth of GDP minus the growth of population.

Leisure: producing the same output in fewer hours is a gain GDP does not show.
The environment: pollution and the using up of natural resources are not subtracted.

The underground economy: unreported work is missed.
Quality and new goods: better products at the same price are hard to measure.

blocks.html: Even so, GDP per person moves closely with many things people care about, such as life expectancy, health and education, which is why economists still use it, alongside other measures.

blocks.html: GDP is measured in dollars (GDP = C + I + G + NX), and the value of a dollar changes as prices rise. If GDP grows 6% in a year, did the economy make 6% more stuff, or did prices go up? To separate the two, we need percent change and a fixed set of prices.

Nominal GDP values each year's output at that year's prices. Real GDP values each year's output at the prices of one base year. Because the prices are held fixed, real GDP changes only when the quantities produced change.

Suppose an economy makes only pizzas. Last year it made 100 at \$10; this year it makes 100 at \$12. Nominal GDP rose from \$1,000 to \$1,200, a 20% rise, yet not one more pizza was made. Valuing this year's 100 pizzas at last year's \$10 price gives real GDP of \$1,000: no growth, which matches what happened. Real GDP answers "how much did we make?"; nominal GDP mixes that with "how much did prices change?"

steps: Real 2023 (base year): $10 \times 100 + 20 \times 50 = 2{,}000$.
Real growth: $\dfrac{2{,}090 - 2{,}000}{2{,}000} \times 100 = 4.5\%$. Nominal grew $\dfrac{2{,}195 - 2{,}000}{2{,}000} \times 100 = 9.75\%$; the rest was higher prices.

blocks.title: A shortcut
blocks.q: Nominal GDP rose 7% and prices rose 3%. About how much did real output grow?
steps: Real growth $\approx$ nominal growth − inflation.

blocks.html: Reading a rise in nominal GDP as more production. It may be only higher prices. Check: when you see a GDP number, ask "nominal or real?" Growth comparisons over time should use real GDP.

blocks.html: Once you have nominal and real GDP (Nominal and Real GDP), their ratio measures how much prices have changed since the base year. That ratio is the GDP deflator, a price index for everything the economy produces.

$$\text{GDP deflator} = \dfrac{\text{nominal GDP}}{\text{real GDP}} \times 100$$ It equals 100 in the base year. A deflator of 115 means prices of the economy's output are 15% higher than in the base year. Rearranged, $\text{real GDP} = \dfrac{\text{nominal GDP}}{\text{deflator}/100}$.

Nominal GDP is current quantities at current prices; real GDP is the same quantities at base-year prices. The quantities are the same on top and bottom, so they cancel out, and what is left compares current prices with base-year prices for the very same output. Multiplying by 100 turns the ratio into an index. In the base year, nominal and real GDP are equal, so the deflator is exactly 100.

blocks.html: Labor is one of the factors of production. When labor sits idle, the economy produces less than it could. To measure idle labor, the government first has to sort every adult into groups, using careful definitions.

The labor force is everyone who is employed plus everyone who is unemployed. Unemployed means: no job, available for work, and actively looked for work in the past four weeks (or on temporary layoff, waiting to be recalled). Adults who are neither are not in the labor force.

The point is to measure people who want to work and cannot find a job. A retiree or a full-time student who is not looking is not "unused labor" in that sense; counting them as unemployed would make the number swing with the age of the population and with school enrollment. So the survey asks about behavior: did you work for pay, and if not, did you look for work?

In the United States, the Bureau of Labor Statistics runs the monthly Current Population Survey of about 60,000 households. It counts civilians 16 and older who are not in prisons, nursing homes or other institutions. Anyone who did any paid work in the survey week counts as employed, even one hour of part-time work.

blocks.html: With adults sorted into groups (Who Is in the Labor Force), the unemployment rate is a percent: what share of the labor force is unemployed.
$$\text{unemployment rate} = \dfrac{\text{unemployed}}{\text{labor force}} \times 100$$ $$\text{labor force participation rate} = \dfrac{\text{labor force}}{\text{adult population}} \times 100$$

The unemployment rate asks: of the people who want to work, what share cannot find a job? So the denominator is the labor force, not all adults. The participation rate answers a different question: what share of adults are working or looking? Watching both together tells a fuller story. If unemployed people give up looking, they leave the labor force: both the top and the bottom of the unemployment fraction shrink, and the rate falls even though no one found a job.

blocks.title: The rate, not the count
blocks.q: A country has 250 million adults: 152 million employed, 8 million unemployed, the rest not in the labor force. Find the unemployment rate and the participation rate.
steps: Labor force $= 152 + 8 = 160$ million.
Unemployment rate $= \dfrac{8}{160} \times 100 = 5\%$.
Participation rate $= \dfrac{160}{250} \times 100 = 64\%$.
Dividing 8 by all 250 million adults would give 3.2%, which is wrong.

blocks.title: Discouraged workers
blocks.q: There are 92 million employed and 8 million unemployed. Then 2 million of the unemployed stop looking. Find the new unemployment rate.
steps: Before: $\dfrac{8}{100} \times 100 = 8\%$.
After: unemployed $= 6$ million; labor force $= 98$ million.
$\dfrac{6}{98} \times 100 \approx 6.1\%$. The rate fell by almost 2 points, yet no one found work.

blocks.html: Dividing by the whole adult population, and missing that discouraged workers leaving the labor force can lower the rate. Check: your denominator should be employed + unemployed. When the rate falls, ask whether employment rose or people stopped looking.

blocks.html: The The Unemployment Rate is never zero, even in a booming economy. Economists sort unemployment by its cause, because different causes call for different responses.

Frictional unemployment: people between jobs, searching for a good match. Structural unemployment: a mismatch between workers' skills or locations and the jobs available. Cyclical unemployment: job losses from a fall in spending across the economy in a recession. The natural rate of unemployment = frictional + structural; at "full employment," cyclical unemployment is zero.

In a growing, changing economy, people quit to find better jobs, graduates look for their first job, and families move. Searching takes time, so some frictional unemployment is normal and even healthy: it means people are finding better matches. Industries also rise and fall, so some workers' skills stop matching what employers want. That structural unemployment can last longer and may need retraining. Neither goes away when the economy is strong. Only cyclical unemployment comes from too little total spending, which is why the natural rate is above zero.

blocks.html: Nominal and Real GDP needed fixed prices to remove inflation from output. To measure inflation itself for households, economists price a fixed basket of the things a typical family buys, year after year.

A price index compares the cost of a fixed basket with its cost in a base period, which is set to 100: $$\text{index} = \dfrac{\text{cost of the basket this period}}{\text{cost of the basket in the base period}} \times 100$$ The consumer price index (CPI), from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, uses a basket of goods and services bought by urban households.

Holding the basket fixed means only prices can change the cost, so the index measures price changes alone. Setting the base period to 100 turns the ratio into an easy percent: an index of 120 means the same basket costs 20% more than in the base period. An index has no dollar units: 120 is not \$120.

blocks.title: Building an index
blocks.q: A basket is 10 loaves of bread and 15 gallons of gas. In 2022 bread is \$2.50 and gas \$3.00; in 2024 bread is \$2.90 and gas \$3.40. With 2022 as the base year, find the 2024 index.
steps: Cost in 2022: $10 \times 2.50 + 15 \times 3.00 = 25 + 45 = 70$ dollars.
Cost in 2024 (same basket): $10 \times 2.90 + 15 \times 3.40 = 29 + 51 = 80$ dollars.
Index $= \dfrac{80}{70} \times 100 \approx 114.3$. The basket costs about 14.3% more.

steps: The base period is 100.
$135 - 100 = 35$: the basket costs 35% more than in the base period. It does not mean anything costs \$135.

blocks.text: Why the CPI tends to run a little high

Quality changes: a phone that costs the same but does much more is a better deal, which is hard to count.
New goods: new products enter the basket only after a delay.

blocks.html: Each of these makes the CPI rise somewhat faster than the true cost of living. The Bureau of Labor Statistics has changed its methods to shrink these biases, but some remain.
Reading an index of 120 as a price of \$120, and missing that a fixed basket tends to overstate inflation. Check: subtract 100 from the index to get the percent change since the base period.

blocks.html: A Price Indexes and the CPI tells you the price level. The inflation rate tells you how fast it is changing, using Percent Increase and Decrease.

$$\text{inflation rate} = \dfrac{\text{index this period} - \text{index last period}}{\text{index last period}} \times 100$$ Inflation: the price level rises. Deflation: the price level falls (negative inflation). Disinflation: inflation slows down, but prices still rise.

The inflation rate is the slope of the price level, not its height. Think of a car's speed: slowing from 60 to 30 miles per hour is still moving forward. In the same way, when inflation falls from 6% to 2%, prices are still climbing, just more slowly. Only when the rate goes below zero does the price level itself fall.

steps: Year 3: $\dfrac{110 - 106}{106} \times 100 \approx 3.8\%$.
Inflation fell from 6% to about 3.8%, but stayed positive: disinflation. Prices still rose.

blocks.html: How much inflation is normal? The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2% a year over the longer run, measured with a close cousin of the CPI (the price index for personal consumption expenditures). A little steady inflation leaves room to cut interest rates in a slump; long stretches of deflation are rare and tend to come with weak economies.

Thinking falling inflation means falling prices. Disinflation means prices still rise, only more slowly; deflation means the price level falls. Check: look at the price index itself. Is it still going up? Then it is not deflation.

blocks.html: Is a \$15 hourly wage today better than \$10 an hour twenty years ago? It depends on how much prices rose in between. The Inflation, Deflation and Disinflation and the price index let you compare dollars from different years.

To express an amount in base-year dollars, divide by the index over 100: $$\text{real value} = \dfrac{\text{nominal value}}{\text{index}/100}$$ To move an amount from year A's dollars into year B's dollars: $$\text{amount}_B = \text{amount}_A \times \dfrac{\text{index}_B}{\text{index}_A}$$

An index of 150 means prices are 1.5 times base-year prices. So a \$30 wage at that time buys what \$20 bought in the base year: $30 \div 1.5 = 20$. Dividing takes the price rise out. Multiplying instead would put a second dose of inflation in, making the old wage look even bigger, which is backwards. The ratio form works the same way: it scales by how much prices changed between the two years.

blocks.html: Higher prices sound bad for everyone. But prices are also incomes: the price of labor is a wage. Using Converting Nominal to Real, we can see who really loses from inflation, and when.

Unexpected inflation moves buying power from lenders to borrowers and hurts people whose incomes or savings are fixed in dollars. All inflation brings costs such as menu costs (changing posted prices), shoe-leather costs (effort spent holding less cash) and confusion about values over time.

A loan is a promise to repay a fixed number of dollars. If prices rise faster than both sides expected when they agreed on the interest rate, the dollars repaid buy less than planned: the borrower gains and the lender loses. If inflation is expected, the lender builds it into the interest rate, so neither side is surprised. Meanwhile, when wages rise along with prices, workers' buying power does not fall: real income depends on wages compared with prices, not on prices alone.

steps: Real wage growth $\approx 5\% - 5\% = 0\%$.

blocks.html: Some incomes are protected by indexing: U.S. Social Security benefits are raised each year with a price index. Other costs remain: firms spend effort changing prices, people hold less cash, and when the value of a dollar keeps shifting, it is harder to compare prices and profits over time and to plan.

Thinking inflation makes everyone poorer by the inflation rate. When wages rise along with prices, real income need not fall, and surprise inflation helps borrowers while it hurts lenders. Check: compare the growth of each person's income (or the interest they pay or earn) with the inflation rate.

blocks.html: Nominal and Real GDP does not grow smoothly. It rises for a while, then falls, then rises again. These swings change jobs (cyclical unemployment) and are called the business cycle. On a production possibilities curve, a recession is like moving to a point inside the curve.

The business cycle has four phases: expansion (real GDP rises), peak (the high point), contraction (real GDP falls; a recession when it is large and lasting), and trough (the low point). Over the long run, real GDP moves around a rising trend of potential output, what the economy can produce with its resources fully employed.

Spending, hiring and production feed one another: when spending rises, firms hire, and new paychecks raise spending again; when spending falls, the same loop runs in reverse. Meanwhile the economy's capacity grows steadily with more capital, workers and better technology. Real GDP can run below potential (a recessionary gap) or, for a while, above it (an inflationary gap), when workers and factories are pushed past their normal pace.

blocks.name: ec-cycle
blocks.cap: Drag the gold marker to read the phase and the output gap. Red shading: output below potential; gold shading: above potential.

blocks.title: Reading the phases
blocks.q: Real GDP (billions of base-year dollars) for six years: 100, 103, 106, 104, 102, 105. Name the phase in each part.
steps: Years 1 to 3: real GDP rises, an expansion.
Year 3 (106) is higher than the years on either side: the peak.
Years 3 to 5: real GDP falls, a contraction.
Year 5 (102) is the lowest point: the trough. After it, a new expansion begins.

blocks.html: In the United States, the National Bureau of Economic Research dates recessions. It looks for a significant decline in activity spread across the economy and lasting more than a few months, using jobs, income and spending as well as GDP. "Two quarters in a row of falling real GDP" is a common rule of thumb, not the official definition.

Confusing slower growth with a recession, or thinking potential output is the most an economy could ever produce. If real GDP grows 1% after growing 3%, the economy is still expanding. And output can run above potential for a while, with overtime and extra shifts. Check: is real GDP actually falling?

blocks.html: For one good, demand slopes down: a higher price, and buyers want less. Aggregate demand looks similar, but it plots something different: the total real GDP that households, firms, government and foreigners want to buy (C + I + G + NX) at each price level, measured by a Price Indexes and the CPI.

Aggregate demand (AD) slopes down. A lower price level raises the quantity of real GDP demanded because of three effects: the wealth effect, the interest-rate effect and the exchange-rate (foreign purchases) effect. A change in the price level is a movement along AD.

When the whole price level falls, there is no cheaper domestic good to switch to, so the single-market reason does not apply. Instead: (1) Wealth: the money and savings people hold buy more, so they feel richer and spend more. (2) Interest rates: people need less money for their purchases and lend out the rest, interest rates fall, and firms and families borrow to buy machines, homes and cars. (3) Exchange rate: our goods get cheaper next to foreign goods, so exports rise and imports fall. A higher price level runs all three in reverse.

blocks.html: Just as with demand for one good, there is a difference between moving along AD and shifting it. A change in the price level moves along Aggregate Demand. Anything else that changes spending at every price level shifts the curve.

AD shifts right (an increase) when consumption, investment, government purchases or net exports rise at every price level, and left when they fall. A change in the price level is a movement along AD, not a shift.

AD is the sum $C + I + G + NX$ at each price level. If households feel more confident, they buy more at every price level, so every point on the curve moves right. The same holds for each component. The price level is the variable on the vertical axis, so changing it only slides the economy to another point on the same curve.

blocks.html: When income rises, how much more do people spend? The answer drives the multiplier in the next lesson. It is a rate of change: the change in spending per dollar of change in income. Consumption is the largest part of GDP.

$$MPC = \dfrac{\Delta C}{\Delta Y} \qquad MPS = \dfrac{\Delta S}{\Delta Y} \qquad MPC + MPS = 1$$ Here $Y$ is disposable (after-tax) income. The MPC is the share of an extra dollar that is spent; the MPS is the share that is saved.

Each extra dollar of disposable income can only be spent or saved, so the two shares add to 1. If you spend 80 cents of an extra dollar, you save 20 cents: MPC = 0.8, MPS = 0.2. The word "marginal" means "extra": it is about the change, not the total. A family can spend 95% of its whole income but only 80% of a raise. On a graph of consumption against income, the MPC is the slope.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: A consumption line against disposable income: $a$ is spending at zero income, and the slope $b$ is the MPC. Raise $b$ and each extra dollar of income adds more spending.

blocks.title: From changes
blocks.q: When income rises from \$500 to \$600 a week, spending rises from \$470 to \$545. Find the MPC and MPS.
steps: $\Delta Y = 100$ and $\Delta C = 75$.
Not $\dfrac{545}{600} \approx 0.91$: that is the share of total income spent (the average propensity to consume).

blocks.title: Using the MPC
blocks.q: The MPC is 0.9 and disposable income rises by \$200 billion. How much do consumption and saving rise?
steps: $\Delta C = 0.9 \times 200 = 180$ billion dollars.
$\Delta S = 0.1 \times 200 = 20$ billion dollars. Check: $180 + 20 = 200$.
blocks.a: C up \$180 billion; S up \$20 billion

blocks.html: Computing the MPC as total spending over total income. The MPC uses changes: $\Delta C \div \Delta Y$. Check: the MPC must be between 0 and 1, and MPC + MPS must equal exactly 1.

blocks.html: Suppose the government buys \$100 billion more of goods. That \$100 billion becomes someone's income, and they spend part of it, set by the MPC. That spending becomes someone else's income, and so on. Adding these rounds needs a little decimal arithmetic.

$$\text{spending multiplier} = \dfrac{1}{1 - MPC} = \dfrac{1}{MPS}$$ With the price level unchanged, a change in autonomous spending ($G$, $I$, exports, or consumption not caused by income) changes real GDP by the multiplier times that change.

With $MPC = 0.8$, a first \$100 of new spending creates \$100 of income. Then \$80 is spent, then \$64, then \$51.20, and so on: each round is 0.8 times the last. The total is a geometric series: $$100 + 100(0.8) + 100(0.8)^2 + \cdots = \dfrac{100}{1 - 0.8} = 500.$$ The rounds shrink because at each step the MPS share is saved and leaves the chain. A bigger MPC means less leaks out each round, so the multiplier is bigger.

blocks.name: ec-multiplier
blocks.cap: Each bar is one round of spending; the green line is the running total, which climbs toward the gold limit. Press Play, or change the MPC.

blocks.title: Finding the change in GDP
blocks.q: The MPC is 0.75 and investment rises by \$40 billion. With the price level unchanged, how much does real GDP rise?
steps: Multiplier $= \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.75} = \dfrac{1}{0.25} = 4$.
$\Delta GDP = 4 \times 40 = 160$ billion dollars.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: A \$50 billion rise in government purchases raises real GDP by \$250 billion. What is the MPC?
steps: Multiplier $= \dfrac{250}{50} = 5$.
$\dfrac{1}{MPS} = 5$, so $MPS = 0.2$ and $MPC = 0.8$.

blocks.title: It works in reverse
blocks.q: The MPS is 0.25. Business investment falls by \$20 billion. With the price level unchanged, how does real GDP change?
steps: Multiplier $= \dfrac{1}{0.25} = 4$.
$\Delta GDP = 4 \times (-20) = -80$ billion dollars. Lost spending is lost income, which cuts spending again in every round.

blocks.html: This simple multiplier assumes prices stay put and that only saving leaks out. In real economies taxes and imports also leak out of each round, and prices may rise, so measured multipliers are smaller. How large they are in practice is one of the questions economists debate.

Using the MPC itself as the multiplier, or dividing 1 by the MPC instead of by the MPS. With $MPC = 0.8$ the multiplier is 5, not 0.8 and not 1.25. Check: the multiplier is always at least 1, and it grows as the MPC grows.

blocks.html: Fiscal policy can also change taxes. A tax cut works through the same rounds as the The Spending Multiplier, with one difference at the start.

$$\text{tax multiplier} = -\dfrac{MPC}{MPS}$$ A tax cut of $\Delta T$ raises real GDP by $\dfrac{MPC}{MPS} \times \Delta T$ (with the price level unchanged); a tax increase lowers it. Transfer payments work like a tax cut. A change in $G$ matched by an equal change in taxes has a balanced-budget multiplier of 1.

When the government buys \$100 of goods, the first round is \$100 of spending. When it cuts taxes by \$100, households save part before spending anything: with $MPC = 0.8$, the first round is only \$80. After that, the rounds are the same, each 0.8 times the last. So the total is $80 \times 5 = 400$, which is $\dfrac{0.8}{0.2} \times 100$. The tax multiplier (4 here) is exactly one less than the spending multiplier (5). The minus sign says that raising taxes lowers GDP.

blocks.name: ec-multiplier
blocks.cap: A \$100 tax cut: round 1 is only MPC × \$100, because part of the cut is saved. Compare the limit with the spending multiplier's.

blocks.title: A tax increase
blocks.q: The MPC is 0.75. Taxes rise by \$40 billion. With the price level unchanged, how does real GDP change?
steps: Tax multiplier $= -\dfrac{0.75}{0.25} = -3$.
$\Delta GDP = -3 \times 40 = -120$ billion dollars.

blocks.title: Spending versus tax cut
blocks.q: The MPC is 0.9. Which raises GDP more: \$10 billion more in government purchases or a \$10 billion tax cut? By how much?
steps: Spending: $\dfrac{1}{0.1} \times 10 = 100$.
Tax cut: $\dfrac{0.9}{0.1} \times 10 = 90$.
Purchases raise GDP \$10 billion more: the first round the government spends directly.

blocks.title: Balanced budget
blocks.q: The government raises purchases by \$50 billion and raises taxes by \$50 billion. MPC = 0.8.
steps: Purchases: $+5 \times 50 = +250$. Taxes: $-4 \times 50 = -200$.
Net: $+50$ billion, the size of the spending change.

blocks.html: Using the spending multiplier for a tax change, forgetting that part of a tax cut is saved before any spending happens, or missing the sign: a tax increase lowers GDP. Check: the tax multiplier's size is one less than the spending multiplier's, and its sign is opposite to the tax change.

blocks.html: Aggregate Demand is half of the model. The other half is supply: how much real GDP firms produce at each price level. Its shifters echo the shifters of supply for one good, now for the whole economy.

Short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) slopes up: a higher price level brings more output in the short run, because wages and some other input prices are slow to change. SRAS shifts with production costs: nominal wages, energy and other input prices, productivity, business taxes and subsidies, and supply shocks.

Many costs are fixed in the short run by contracts and habit: wages are set for a year, rent for a lease. If the prices firms sell at rise while those costs stay put, each extra unit becomes more profitable, so firms produce more: an upward slope. When a cost itself changes, firms need a different price level to produce any given output, so the whole curve moves. Higher oil prices move SRAS up and to the left: at every price level, less output. That is a decrease in SRAS, even though the curve moved "up."

blocks.title: Shift or movement?
blocks.q: What happens to SRAS? (a) Nominal wages rise across the economy. (b) The price level rises while wages stay fixed. (c) A new technology lowers costs in many industries.
steps: (a) A cost rises: SRAS shifts left (a decrease).
(b) The price level is on the axis: a movement up along SRAS.
(c) Lower costs per unit: SRAS shifts right (an increase).

blocks.title: Reading the shift
blocks.q: After a drought, the SRAS curve moves up by 5 price-level points at every output. Is that an increase or a decrease in SRAS?
steps: Read the shift sideways: at any given price level, firms now produce less.
So it is a decrease, a shift to the left.

blocks.html: Shifting SRAS when the price level changes, or calling higher input costs an "increase" in SRAS because the curve moves up. A price-level change is a movement along SRAS, and higher costs mean less output at each price level: a decrease. Check: read supply shifts horizontally.

blocks.html: Short-Run Aggregate Supply slopes up because some costs are sticky. Given enough time, though, wages and other costs catch up with prices. Then the economy's output depends only on what it can produce, as on the production possibilities curve, with unemployment at its natural rate.

Long-run aggregate supply (LRAS) is a vertical line at full-employment (potential) output. It shifts only when the economy's capacity changes: more or better resources (labor, capital, land), better technology, or better institutions.

Suppose all prices and all wages double. Each worker's pay buys the same as before, each firm's profit per unit is the same in real terms, so no one has a reason to work or produce more. Real output stays where resources and technology put it. That is why LRAS is vertical: in the long run the price level does not change real output. Producing on LRAS matches producing on the PPC; a recessionary gap is like a point inside the curve, and growth shifts both outward.

blocks.cap: Press the growth button: more capital, better technology or more workers shift LRAS and SRAS right together. The price level does not move LRAS.

blocks.name: ec-ppc
blocks.cap: The same growth on a production possibilities curve: the whole curve moves outward.

blocks.title: What shifts LRAS?
blocks.q: Which shift LRAS? (a) A wave of new factories and machines. (b) The price level rises 10%. (c) Government purchases rise.
steps: (a) More capital raises potential output: LRAS shifts right.
(b) The price level does not change capacity: no shift.
(c) More spending shifts AD, not capacity: no LRAS shift.

blocks.title: Where output ends up
blocks.q: Potential output is \$20 trillion. Demand rises and output briefly reaches \$21 trillion. Where is output in the long run?
steps: Wages and costs catch up, SRAS shifts left, and output returns to LRAS.
Long-run output is \$20 trillion, at a higher price level.

blocks.html: Drawing LRAS sloping up, or shifting it when demand changes. LRAS moves only when the economy's capacity to produce changes. Check: ask "does this change the resources, technology or institutions the economy has?"

blocks.html: Put the three curves together: AD, SRAS and LRAS. Where AD meets SRAS is the short-run equilibrium. Comparing it with LRAS tells you where the economy sits in the The Business Cycle.

Short-run equilibrium is where AD = SRAS. If equilibrium output is below full-employment output (left of LRAS), there is a recessionary gap; if it is above (right of LRAS), an inflationary gap. Long-run equilibrium is where all three curves meet.

At the AD–SRAS crossing, the output buyers want equals the output firms want to produce at that price level, so there is no pressure to change. But that output need not equal potential. Below potential, workers are idle and cyclical unemployment is high. Above potential, firms run overtime and labor is scarce, unemployment is below its natural rate, and wages and prices are pushed up.

blocks.name: ec-adas
blocks.cap: The economy starts with a recessionary gap (red): AD crosses SRAS left of LRAS. Try demand and supply shocks and watch the gap change.

blocks.title: Naming the gap
blocks.q: Full-employment output is \$20 trillion. Short-run equilibrium output is \$21 trillion.
steps: Equilibrium is to the right of LRAS: output is above potential.
An inflationary gap of \$1 trillion; unemployment is below its natural rate.

blocks.title: Solving with equations
blocks.q: AD: $P = 200 - 5Y$ and SRAS: $P = 80 + 5Y$ ($Y$ in trillions). Full-employment output is 13. Find equilibrium.
steps: Set them equal: $200 - 5Y = 80 + 5Y$, so $120 = 10Y$ and $Y = 12$.
$12 < 13$: a recessionary gap of \$1 trillion.

blocks.html: The gaps also tell you about jobs. Fewer goods and services take fewer workers, so a recessionary gap comes with unemployment above its natural rate; an inflationary gap comes with unemployment below it, and with wages and prices under upward pressure. The next lessons show what happens to a gap over time, and what policy can do about it.

Mixing up the gaps, for example calling output above full employment a recessionary gap. Check: "recessionary" goes with less output and more unemployment, so it must be left of LRAS; "inflationary" goes with overheating, right of LRAS.

blocks.html: Starting from Equilibrium and Output Gaps, any event that shifts a curve moves the economy to a new short-run equilibrium. The direction of the change depends on which curve moved.

A demand shock (AD shifts) moves the price level and real GDP in the same direction. A supply shock (SRAS shifts) moves them in opposite directions. A negative supply shock brings stagflation: a higher price level with falling output and rising unemployment.

AD slopes down and SRAS slopes up. If AD shifts right, the economy slides up along SRAS: more output, higher prices. If SRAS shifts left, the economy slides up along AD: higher prices, but less output. So the pattern of the change tells you which kind of shock hit. In the 1970s, oil price jumps raised prices while output fell, a clear supply shock.

blocks.html: After a shock, the economy may sit in a gap. If no one changes policy, does it stay there? In the AD–AS model the answer is no, eventually, because sticky wages and prices do not stay sticky forever.

In a recessionary gap, unemployment is high, so over time nominal wages and other input prices fall; SRAS shifts right until output returns to full employment at a lower price level. In an inflationary gap, wages rise; SRAS shifts left until output returns to full employment at a higher price level. The self-correcting move is a shift of SRAS, not of LRAS or AD.

Wages respond to the job market. With many people looking for work, firms can fill jobs at lower pay, and workers accept smaller raises; as labor costs fall, firms produce more at every price level. With labor scarce, the reverse happens. In both cases the adjustment stops only when output is back at potential, because only there is the job market neither slack nor tight. LRAS does not move: capacity did not change.

The economy ends where AD meets LRAS: $Y = 12$, $P = 180 - 5(12) = 120$.
The price level falls from $180 - 5(10) = 130$ to 120.

steps: Labor is scarce, so nominal wages rise.
SRAS shifts left until output returns to potential, at a higher price level.
blocks.a: SRAS shifts left; prices rise; output returns to potential

blocks.html: How fast does this happen? Here economists disagree. Many find that wages fall slowly in a recession (because of contracts, minimum wages and concerns about fairness), so adjustment can take years; that is the case for using fiscal or monetary policy to speed recovery. Others stress that policy acts with delays and can overshoot. Both sides agree on the direction of the adjustment; they differ on its speed and on what policy should do.

blocks.html: A demand shock can leave the economy in a gap. Fiscal policy is the government's use of spending and taxes to push aggregate demand back toward full employment. Its strength depends on the multipliers.

Expansionary fiscal policy (more government purchases, lower taxes, or higher transfer payments) shifts AD right to close a recessionary gap. Contractionary fiscal policy (fewer purchases, higher taxes, lower transfers) shifts AD left to close an inflationary gap. In the United States, Congress and the President set fiscal policy.

Government purchases are part of AD directly. Taxes and transfers change households' disposable income, and so consumption. In a recession, too little spending leaves workers and factories idle; adding spending (or leaving households more to spend) moves output toward potential. In an inflationary gap, the economy is straining; trimming spending eases the pressure on prices.

blocks.html: Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy tells you which way to move. The multipliers tell you how far. Because each dollar of new spending is multiplied, the change needed is much smaller than the gap.

To close a gap with government purchases: $\Delta G = \dfrac{\text{gap}}{\text{spending multiplier}}$. With taxes: $\Delta T = \dfrac{\text{gap}}{MPC/MPS}$ (a cut for a recessionary gap, a rise for an inflationary gap). This simple rule assumes the price level stays about the same.

If the multiplier is 5, every \$1 of new government purchases raises GDP by \$5. To raise GDP by \$100 billion, the government needs only \$20 billion: $20 \times 5 = 100$. Setting the change equal to the whole gap would overshoot. For taxes, the multiplier is smaller ($MPC/MPS$, one less), because households save part of a tax cut before spending, so a larger tax change is needed for the same effect.

blocks.q: A recessionary gap is \$200 billion and the MPC is 0.75. How much should government purchases rise?
steps: Spending multiplier $= \dfrac{1}{0.25} = 4$.

steps: Tax multiplier (size) $= \dfrac{0.75}{0.25} = 3$.

Real-world multipliers are also uncertain, which is one reason economists debate how much fiscal policy to use.

blocks.html: Taxes are one side of fiscal policy, and how they are built matters too. Two rates describe any tax: the share of your total income you pay, and the rate on your next dollar. Both are percents of a number.

Average tax rate = total tax ÷ income. Marginal tax rate = the tax rate on the next dollar of income. A tax is progressive if the average rate rises with income, regressive if it falls, and proportional (flat) if it stays the same.

Under a bracket system, each rate applies only to the income inside its bracket. Picture buckets stacked on top of each other: your income fills the lowest bucket first, then the next. Only the dollars in the top bucket you reach face the top rate. So moving into a higher bracket raises the tax on the dollars above the line, never on the dollars below it. That is why, under bracket rates, a raise always leaves you with more after-tax income, and why the average rate stays below your marginal rate.

blocks.html: Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy usually means a new law. But part of the budget responds to the business cycle on its own, through Progressive, Regressive and Proportional Taxes and programs already on the books.

Automatic stabilizers are parts of existing tax and spending law that cushion the economy without any new decision: progressive income taxes, unemployment insurance, and programs such as food assistance (SNAP) and Medicaid. In a recession they push the budget toward a deficit; in a boom, toward a surplus. Discretionary fiscal policy is a new law passed on purpose.

When incomes fall in a recession, people slip into lower brackets and pay less tax, so disposable income falls by less than income. Laid-off workers collect unemployment insurance, and more families qualify for food assistance. Both keep spending from falling as far as it would have. In a boom the reverse happens: tax collections rise faster than incomes and fewer people need benefits, which cools spending a little. No vote is needed, so there is no delay.

blocks.html: When Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy spends more than it collects, the government borrows the difference. Two words describe this, and they are easy to mix up: one measures a year, the other the total.

The budget deficit is one year's shortfall: spending (purchases, transfers and interest) minus revenue. A surplus is the reverse. The national debt is the total amount the government owes: the running sum of past deficits minus past surpluses. The deficit is a flow; the debt is a stock.

Think of a bathtub. The water level is the debt; the water pouring in each year is the deficit. As long as water flows in, the level rises, even if the faucet is turned down. A smaller deficit means the debt grows more slowly, not that it falls. The level goes down only when water drains out: a surplus. Economists often compare the debt with GDP, because a larger economy can carry a larger debt.

blocks.html: Savers and borrowers meet in financial markets. Two common assets are stocks and bonds. A bond pays interest much like Simple Interest, and its price depends on the percent return that new bonds offer.

A bond is a loan: the buyer lends money to a government or company, which promises fixed interest payments (the coupon) and the face value at maturity. A stock is a share of ownership in a company. When market interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, and when rates fall, bond prices rise.

An old bond's payments are fixed when it is issued. Suppose your bond pays \$50 a year on \$1,000, a 5% coupon. If new bonds now pay 7%, no one will pay \$1,000 for yours: for \$1,000 they could get \$70 a year. Your bond's price must drop until its \$50 a year is as good a deal as a new bond. So bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions. A bond that pays one amount $A$ in a year is worth $\dfrac{A}{1 + r}$ today at market rate $r$: a higher $r$ means a smaller price.

blocks.html: A bond or a bank account pays a nominal interest rate in dollars. But inflation shrinks what each dollar buys. To know what a saver really earns, combine the two, using interest rates and price changes.

$$\text{real interest rate} \approx \text{nominal interest rate} - \text{inflation rate}$$ The nominal rate is the growth of your dollars; the real rate is the growth of your buying power. A lender who wants a real return of $r$ and expects inflation $\pi^e$ charges about $r + \pi^e$.

Lend \$100 at 5% for a year: you get \$105 back. If prices rose 3%, something that cost \$100 now costs \$103, so your \$105 buys only about 2% more than before. Exactly, $\dfrac{1.05}{1.03} - 1 \approx 1.94\%$; for small rates, subtracting is close enough, and this course uses the subtraction rule. If inflation is higher than the nominal rate, the real rate is negative: savers lose buying power even though their balance grows.

blocks.title: Finding the real rate

blocks.title: Expected versus actual
blocks.q: A loan is made at 7%, when both sides expect 2% inflation. Inflation turns out to be 5%. Who gains?
steps: Expected real rate: $7\% - 2\% = 5\%$. Actual: $7\% - 5\% = 2\%$.
The borrower pays a lower real rate than planned and gains; the lender loses.

blocks.html: Real rates matter for decisions. A firm deciding whether to borrow for a new machine compares the machine's return with the real cost of borrowing, because the machine's output will sell at future prices. Savers deciding between spending now and later care about how much more they can buy later: the real return.

Adding inflation instead of subtracting it, or thinking a lender earning 5% gains 5% in buying power when inflation is 3%. Check: if prices rise faster than your balance, your buying power falls, so the real rate must be below the nominal rate when inflation is positive.

blocks.html: Trade makes people better off, but trading directly, goods for goods, is clumsy. A baker who wants shoes has to find a shoemaker who wants bread. Money solves that problem.

Money is anything widely accepted in payment. It does three jobs: a medium of exchange (you trade it for goods and services), a unit of account (prices and values are measured in it) and a store of value (it holds buying power until you spend it).

Under barter, every trade needs a "double coincidence of wants," and every pair of goods needs its own price: with 100 goods there would be $\dfrac{100 \times 99}{2} = 4{,}950$ exchange rates to keep track of. With money, each good needs one price in dollars, and you can sell your labor for money and spend it on anything, now or later. Money need not be backed by gold: today's dollars are fiat money, valuable because people accept them in trade and the government accepts them for taxes.

blocks.html: Money is whatever is accepted in payment, but some assets are closer to spendable than others. A checking balance can be spent today; a bond must first be sold. The Federal Reserve measures money at two levels of liquidity.

M1 = currency held by the public + checking (demand) deposits + other liquid deposits, which since May 2020 include savings deposits. M2 = M1 + small time deposits (certificates of deposit under \$100,000) + retail money market fund balances. M2 contains M1. Stocks, bonds and credit limits are not money.

Liquidity is how quickly and cheaply something can be spent. Currency and checking deposits are as liquid as it gets. Savings deposits used to be counted only in M2, because withdrawals were limited; in 2020 the Federal Reserve dropped that limit and moved savings deposits into M1. (Older textbooks still put savings in M2 only.) Time deposits and money market funds take a step or a short wait to spend, so they are in M2 but not M1. The measures are nested circles, not separate pools.

blocks.html: Most money in M1 is not cash but bank deposits. To see how banks handle them, economists use a simple balance sheet called a T-account.

A bank's assets (what it owns: reserves, loans, securities) equal its liabilities (what it owes: mainly customers' deposits) plus owners' equity. Reserves split into required reserves (reserve ratio × deposits) and excess reserves (everything above that).

When you deposit \$100, the bank owes you \$100 on demand: to the bank, your deposit is a liability. The \$100 of cash it now holds is an asset, a reserve. Both sides rise by \$100, so the T-account still balances. Whatever the bank does next (lend, buy a bond), it only swaps one asset for another or changes both sides together; that is why assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Equity is the cushion that belongs to the bank's owners.

blocks.html: A bank with excess reserves can lend them. When it does, something surprising happens: new money appears.

When banks lend out excess reserves, the loans are spent and deposited in other banks, creating new deposits. In the simple model, each new dollar of excess reserves can support up to $\dfrac{1}{rr}$ dollars of new money, where $rr$ is the reserve ratio: the money multiplier is $\dfrac{1}{rr}$. A single bank can lend only its own excess reserves.

Say $rr = 10\%$ and someone deposits \$1,000 of cash. The money supply has not changed yet: \$1,000 of currency became \$1,000 of deposits. The bank keeps \$100 and lends \$900. The borrower spends it; the seller deposits \$900 in Bank B. Now there is \$1,900 of deposits, while \$900 of the original cash circulates as reserves: \$900 of money is new. Bank B keeps \$90 and lends \$810, and so on. The new money adds up to $$900 + 810 + 729 + \cdots = \dfrac{900}{0.10} = 9{,}000.$$

blocks.html: Like any good, money has a supply and a demand. The "price" of holding money is the interest you give up by not holding a bond instead. Use what you know about shifts and equilibrium, the money supply and nominal interest rates.

In the money market, the nominal interest rate is on the vertical axis. The money supply is vertical, set by the central bank. Money demand slopes down: at a higher interest rate people hold less money. Where they cross sets the nominal interest rate. More money supply lowers the rate; more money demand (from a higher price level or more real GDP) raises it.

People hold money because it is handy for buying things, but cash and checking balances earn little or no interest. The higher the interest rate on bonds, the more it costs to keep wealth in money, so people hold less: money demand slopes down. A change in the interest rate moves people along money demand. Money demand shifts when people need more money at every rate: a higher price level means each purchase takes more dollars, and more real GDP means more purchases. The central bank fixes the quantity of money whatever the rate, so supply is vertical.

blocks.html: The central bank (in the United States, the Federal Reserve) can change bank reserves and interest rates. Its tools work through How Banks Create Money and the The Money Market.

The classic tools: open market operations (buying or selling government bonds), the discount rate (the rate the Fed charges banks for loans), and reserve requirements. Today the Fed also sets interest on reserve balances (IORB). Buying bonds, cutting the discount rate, lowering reserve requirements and cutting IORB are expansionary; the opposites are contractionary.

When the Fed buys a bond from a bank, it pays by adding reserves to the bank's account at the Fed: new money from nowhere, all of it excess reserves, so banks can lend more and interest rates fall. Selling bonds drains reserves and does the reverse. A lower discount rate makes it cheaper for banks to borrow reserves. A lower reserve requirement turns required reserves into excess ones. A lower IORB makes leaving money at the Fed less attractive than lending it, pulling short-term rates down.

blocks.html: The The Central Bank's Tools lesson described the classic tools. Since the 2008 financial crisis, the Federal Reserve has run monetary policy in a different way, because banks now hold plenty of reserves.

When reserves are ample, the federal funds rate (the rate banks charge one another for overnight loans of reserves) is steered mainly by administered rates that the Fed sets: interest on reserve balances (IORB) and the overnight reverse repurchase (ON RRP) rate. The Fed sets a target range for the federal funds rate and moves these rates to keep it there. Open market operations keep reserves ample, but small ones barely move the rate.

A bank will not lend its reserves overnight for much less than it can earn by leaving them at the Fed. So IORB acts like a floor under what banks will accept, and the federal funds rate settles near it. (It can trade a little below IORB, because some lenders in that market, such as government-sponsored enterprises, cannot earn IORB; the ON RRP rate, offered to a wider set of lenders such as money market funds, is set at or near the bottom of the target range.) With reserves plentiful, the demand curve for reserves is flat around that level: adding or removing a few reserves hardly changes the rate. To raise rates, the Fed raises IORB and ON RRP.

blocks.html: Put the pieces together. The central bank changes interest rates; interest rates change spending; spending moves aggregate demand.

Expansionary monetary policy: buy bonds (or cut administered rates) → interest rates fall → investment and other interest-sensitive spending rise → AD shifts right → real GDP and the price level rise, unemployment falls. Contractionary policy runs the chain in reverse.

Lower interest rates make it cheaper to borrow for a new factory, a home or a car, so firms and households spend more at every price level: AD shifts right. Only two links in the chain are shifts: the money supply in the money market, and AD in the AD–AS model. The others are movements along curves: along money demand to the new rate, and along investment demand to a new level of investment.

steps: Reserves and the money supply fall.
Interest rates rise.
Investment and interest-sensitive consumption fall; AD shifts left.

blocks.a: Money supply ↓ → interest rates ↑ → investment ↓ → AD ↓ → output and prices ↓

blocks.html: The Fed steers a very short-term rate. Longer-term rates, like those on mortgages, are set in markets and depend on expected future rates, inflation and risk; they usually follow the Fed's moves, but not one for one. Policy also takes time: its effects on spending can take many months to show up.

Linking the steps in the wrong order, or thinking the central bank directly sets every interest rate, mortgage rates included. Check: start in the money market and end with AD; the Fed sets a short-term policy rate, and other rates respond.

blocks.html: The money market sets the nominal interest rate in the short run. A second market, built like any supply and demand market, shows how saving and borrowing set the Nominal and Real Interest Rates, and how government deficits fit in.

In the loanable funds market, the supply of loanable funds comes from saving (by households, by a government running a surplus, and by foreigners lending here) and the demand comes from borrowing (mainly firms investing, plus a government borrowing to cover a deficit). They set the real interest rate.

Savers lend more when the real return is higher, so supply slopes up. Borrowers invest in projects that pay more than the real interest rate, so at a lower rate more projects are worth doing: demand slopes down. Anything that changes saving at every rate shifts supply; anything that changes borrowing at every rate shifts demand. When the government borrows more, it competes with firms for the same pool of saving, so (in this course's framing) demand shifts right and the real rate rises.

blocks.html: Fiscal policy and monetary policy are set by different people: lawmakers and the central bank. Often both act at once. To predict the result, work out each policy's effects on its own, then combine them.

When two policies push a variable the same way, the direction is clear. When they push it in opposite ways, the result is indeterminate: it depends on which effect is larger. Fiscal expansion raises AD and tends to raise interest rates; monetary expansion raises AD and lowers interest rates.

Each policy moves AD, and fiscal policy also pushes up interest rates (more spending and income raise money demand, and government borrowing competes for saving), while monetary policy moves interest rates directly. Stack the arrows. If both shift AD right, output and the price level rise for sure, but the interest rate gets one push up and one push down, so without sizes you cannot say which way it goes.

blocks.html: Demand shocks move output and the price level the same way. Translate that into the two numbers people watch most, the The Unemployment Rate and the Inflation, Deflation and Disinflation, and you get the Phillips curve.

The short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) shows an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. A shift of AD moves the economy along the SRPC. A supply shock or a change in expected inflation shifts the SRPC. At the natural rate of unemployment, inflation equals expected inflation.

When AD shifts right, firms produce more, so they hire and unemployment falls; at the same time the price level rises faster, so inflation rises. That is a move up and to the left along the SRPC. A negative supply shock raises prices while output falls, so inflation and unemployment rise: the whole curve shifts up and to the right. If people expect more inflation, they build it into wages and prices, so inflation is higher at every unemployment rate: also a shift up.

steps: (a) AD shifts right: unemployment falls, inflation rises: a movement up and to the left along the SRPC.
(b) SRAS shifts left: both inflation and unemployment rise: the SRPC shifts up and to the right.
blocks.a: (a) along the curve; (b) the curve shifts

blocks.html: The curve is named for A. W. Phillips, who in 1958 found that British wages rose faster in years of low unemployment. In the 1970s, supply shocks and rising expectations brought high inflation and high unemployment together, a reminder that the short-run curve can shift.

Shifting the short-run Phillips curve when AD changes. AD shifts move the economy along it, while supply shocks and changes in expected inflation shift it. Check: did both inflation and unemployment move the same way? Then the curve shifted.

blocks.html: The The Short-Run Phillips Curve suggests a menu: a little more inflation for a little less unemployment. But self-adjustment warns that wages and expectations catch up. What happens to the menu in the long run?

The long-run Phillips curve (LRPC) is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment. In the long run, unemployment returns to the natural rate whatever the inflation rate. Only a change in the natural rate (frictional or structural unemployment) shifts the LRPC.

Suppose policy pushes unemployment below the natural rate. Inflation rises above what people expected. Workers and firms notice and come to expect the higher inflation, building it into wages and prices: the SRPC shifts up. To keep unemployment low, policy must push inflation higher still, and expectations follow again. Once policy stops pushing, unemployment returns to the natural rate, but inflation stays at the new, higher expected rate. The tradeoff exists only while inflation surprises people. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps made this argument in the late 1960s, before the 1970s bore it out.

blocks.cap: Step through: policy pushes unemployment below the natural rate, expectations catch up and the SRPC shifts up, and in the end unemployment is back at the natural rate with higher inflation.

Holding unemployment below the natural rate takes inflation that keeps rising.

blocks.html: Why do some countries have runaway inflation while others have little? Connect the money supply with real output and inflation.

The equation of exchange: $$MV = PY$$ $M$ is the money supply, $V$ is velocity (how many times a dollar is spent on final output in a year), $P$ is the price level and $Y$ is real output, so $PY$ is nominal GDP. In growth rates: $$\%\Delta M + \%\Delta V \approx \%\Delta P + \%\Delta Y$$ If velocity is stable, money growing faster than real output raises prices in the long run.

Velocity is defined as $V = \dfrac{PY}{M}$, so $MV = PY$ is true by definition. It becomes a theory when we add an assumption: in the long run, real output is set by resources and technology (LRAS), not by money, and velocity changes slowly. Then extra money cannot buy more real output; it bids up prices. Economists broadly agree that sustained, rapid money growth causes high inflation, and that money is neutral in the long run. How stable velocity is, and so how tightly money growth tracks inflation from year to year, is debated: in some decades velocity has swung a lot.

blocks.cap: The money supply $M$ is across the bottom. With velocity $V$ and real output $Y$ fixed, the price level $P = \dfrac{MV}{Y}$ rises in proportion to the money supply: double $M$ and $P$ doubles. Raise $Y$ and the same money supports a lower price level.

blocks.html: When the government runs a deficit, it borrows in the The Loanable Funds Market market. That borrowing has a side effect on private investment.

Crowding out: government borrowing raises the demand for loanable funds, which raises the real interest rate and reduces private investment. Some of the boost from deficit spending is offset by less private spending, and less investment means less capital for the future.

Saving is a limited pool. When the government borrows more of it, the real interest rate must rise to bring supply and demand back together. At the higher rate, some private projects no longer pay, so firms borrow and invest less. How much is crowded out depends on how strongly saving and investment respond to the interest rate, and on the state of the economy: in a deep recession, with idle resources and weak demand for loans, rates may rise little; near full employment, borrowing competes harder for scarce saving. The size of crowding out in practice is debated.

blocks.html: The last few lessons raised questions the model alone cannot settle: how fast expectations and wages adjust, how tightly money tracks prices, how much Crowding Out happens. Economists who weigh the evidence differently form schools of thought.

Schools of macroeconomic thought agree on much: in the long run, output depends on resources and technology, money is neutral, and sustained high inflation comes from rapid money growth. They differ mainly on how fast wages and prices adjust, and so on how active fiscal and monetary policy should be.

Every school uses the same AD–AS logic. The differences come from evidence that is hard to read: economies are complicated, history does not repeat under controlled conditions, and policies arrive with delays. If wages and prices adjust quickly, gaps close on their own and active policy adds little; if they adjust slowly, recessions can drag on and policy can help. Most economists today borrow from several schools.

blocks.html: Over decades, Nominal and Real GDP per person has risen many times over in the richest countries. That is growth of the economy's capacity, the outward shift of the production possibilities curve. Where does it come from?

Labor productivity is real output per hour of work. Real GDP = output per hour × hours worked, so real GDP grows by about the growth of productivity plus the growth of hours. Lasting gains in living standards come from productivity, which rises with physical capital (machines, buildings, equipment), human capital (skills and education) and technology (better ways of producing).

More hours of work raise output, but there are only so many hours in a week, and more work means less leisure. Output per hour has no such limit. A worker with a better tool, more training, or a smarter method produces more in the same hour. Capital alone runs into diminishing returns: the tenth machine per worker adds less than the first. Technology lifts the whole relationship, so the same capital and skills produce more. That is why economists see new ideas as the deepest source of long-run growth.

blocks.html: Productivity growth of 1% or 2% a year sounds small. But growth compounds, like the exponential growth you have seen in algebra: each year's growth builds on the last.

Rule of 70: a quantity growing at $g$ percent a year doubles in about $$\dfrac{70}{g} \text{ years.}$$ So 2% growth doubles income in about 35 years; 7% doubles it in about 10. The exact doubling time is $\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + g/100)}$, very close for small rates.

Growing at rate $r$ (as a decimal) for $t$ years multiplies a quantity by $(1 + r)^t$. Doubling means $(1 + r)^t = 2$, so $t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$. For small $r$, $\ln(1 + r) \approx r$, and $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$, so $t \approx \dfrac{0.69}{r} = \dfrac{69}{g}$ with $g$ in percent. Rounding to 70 makes the arithmetic easy. Adding a fixed amount each year instead would badly understate the result: growth is a percent of an ever larger base.

blocks.html: Adding growth year by year instead of compounding it, which badly underestimates how small differences in growth rates add up over decades. 10% a year for 20 years is not "200% more" but about 6.7 times the start. Check: use the rule of 70 and count doublings.

blocks.html: Productivity and Growth drives long-run growth, and growth shows up as rightward shifts of LRAS and outward shifts of the PPC. Which policies can speed it up?

Policies that build physical capital, human capital and technology, or that improve the institutions that support them, raise potential output: they shift LRAS (and the PPC) outward. Policies that only raise spending shift AD; they do not raise potential output unless they add to the economy's capacity to produce.

Potential output depends on what the economy has to work with and how well it uses it. A tax rebate spent on consumer goods raises demand for a while, but leaves the economy with the same machines, skills and ideas. Building a port does both: the construction spending raises AD now, and the finished port lets firms produce and ship more later. Economists broadly agree on the sources of growth; they debate which particular policies deliver them best and at what cost.

blocks.html: Trade between countries shows up in GDP as net exports. The balance of payments is the full record of a country's dealings with the rest of the world: not just goods, but income and assets too.

The current account records trade in goods and services, income earned on investments abroad, and transfers (like money sent home to family). The financial account records purchases of assets across borders: stocks, bonds, factories, buildings. A small capital account records some capital transfers. Together they balance: current account + capital account + financial account = 0. This course uses the AP convention: a net inflow of foreign capital is a financial account surplus.

Every international purchase is paid for somehow. If Americans buy \$100 more of goods from abroad than they sell, foreigners end up with \$100 of extra dollars. They do not throw them away: they use them to buy U.S. assets, such as Treasury bonds, stocks or real estate. So a current account deficit of \$100 is matched by a financial account surplus of \$100: the country is selling assets to (or borrowing from) the rest of the world. In real data a statistical discrepancy is needed to make the books balance exactly.

blocks.html: To buy something from another country, you usually need its currency. An exchange rate is just a price, and converting between currencies is a proportion.

An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as 0.90 euros per dollar. Always read the units. If the number of euros per dollar rises, each dollar buys more euros: the dollar has appreciated and the euro has depreciated. The two ways of quoting are reciprocals: 0.90 euros per dollar is about 1.11 dollars per euro.

"Euros per dollar" is the price of a dollar, in euros. When that price goes up, the dollar is worth more: it appreciated. The same move, seen from the other side, makes the euro cheaper in dollars. Converting is unit cancelling: $\$200 \times 0.90 \dfrac{\text{euros}}{\text{dollar}} = 180$ euros. Mixing up which currency is "per" is the most common error, so write the units every time.

blocks.html: Exchange rates are prices (Exchange Rates), set by supply and demand like any market price. The question is who supplies and who demands a currency.

In the market for dollars, demand comes from foreigners who need dollars to buy U.S. goods, services and assets. Supply comes from Americans who sell dollars to buy foreign goods, services and assets. Every trade has a mirror: demand for dollars by Europeans is a supply of euros, and supply of dollars by Americans is a demand for euros.

A European tourist in New York must pay in dollars, so she trades euros for dollars: she demands dollars and supplies euros in the same trade. An American buying a French watch trades dollars for euros: he supplies dollars and demands euros. The price on the vertical axis of the dollar market is euros per dollar; in the euro market it is dollars per euro, the reciprocal. Whatever happens in one market shows up, mirrored, in the other.

blocks.html: Now shift the curves in the The Foreign Exchange Market. The usual shifters connect to ideas from earlier units: real interest rates and inflation.

The main shifters of demand for and supply of a currency: tastes for a country's goods, relative incomes, relative price levels (inflation) and relative real interest rates, plus speculation and central bank purchases. For the dollar: higher U.S. real interest rates or higher foreign incomes raise demand for dollars (appreciation); higher U.S. incomes or higher U.S. inflation push the dollar down (depreciation).

Ask who now wants more or fewer dollars. If U.S. real interest rates rise, foreign savers want U.S. bonds and must buy dollars: demand rises. If Europeans get richer, they buy more of everything, U.S. goods included: demand for dollars rises. If Americans get richer, they buy more imports and sell dollars to do it: supply rises. If U.S. prices rise faster than Europe's, U.S. goods look expensive: Europeans want fewer dollars and Americans supply more to buy cheaper European goods. Both push the dollar down.

blocks.html: Exchange rates matter for the whole economy because they change the prices of exports and imports, and so aggregate demand. Use what you learned in What Moves Exchange Rates.

When the dollar appreciates, U.S. goods get dearer abroad and foreign goods get cheaper here: exports fall, imports rise, net exports fall and AD shifts left. When the dollar depreciates, net exports rise and AD shifts right.

A \$50 pair of U.S.-made boots costs a European $50 \times 0.80 = 40$ euros at 0.80 euros per dollar, but $50 \times 1.10 = 55$ euros at 1.10. Same boots, same dollar price, but 15 euros dearer to the buyer. Europeans buy fewer. Meanwhile each dollar buys more euros, so European goods get cheaper for Americans, who buy more of them. Exports fall, imports rise, NX falls. A strong currency helps some people (importers, tourists abroad, buyers of imports) and hurts others (exporters and firms competing with imports); it is not simply "good" or "bad."

blocks.html: The effect works through the whole economy. A currency that depreciates in a slump makes the country's goods cheaper abroad, which cushions the fall in AD; a currency that soars can slow growth by squeezing exporters. For the dollar, these changes come from the market: its value floats, and U.S. authorities have rarely bought or sold currencies to steer it in recent decades. The effects also take time, because buyers need months to switch suppliers.

Assuming a strong currency is always good for a country's output, missing its effect on exporters. Check: follow the chain: stronger dollar → U.S. goods dearer abroad → exports fall, imports rise → NX and AD fall.

blocks.html: Savers can lend across borders. That links the The Loanable Funds Market market with the foreign exchange market.

A higher real interest rate in a country draws in foreign financial capital. To buy that country's assets, foreign savers must first buy its currency, so demand for the currency rises and it appreciates. The inflow also adds to the supply of loanable funds there. A lower real rate sends capital out and the currency depreciates.

Savers look for the best return for the risk. If U.S. bonds pay a higher real rate than similar European bonds, European savers want U.S. bonds, and they need dollars to buy them. That raises demand for dollars. The classic chain for a U.S. budget deficit: the government borrows more → the real interest rate rises → foreign capital flows in → the dollar appreciates → U.S. exports get dearer and imports cheaper → net exports fall. In the loanable funds market, the same inflow adds to supply, which keeps the rate from rising as much as it otherwise would.

blocks.html: The The Balance of Payments and the The Loanable Funds Market market are two views of one fact: a country's saving must pay for its investment, at home or abroad.

$$S_{private} + (T - G) = I + NX$$ Private saving plus the government's budget balance (national saving) equals domestic investment plus net exports. When national saving falls short of investment, net exports are negative: the country borrows the difference from abroad and runs a trade deficit.

Start from $Y = C + I + G + NX$. Households' income is spent, taxed or saved: $Y = C + S_{private} + T$ (with $T$ as taxes net of transfers). Set the two equal and cancel $C$: $S_{private} + T = I + G + NX$, so $S_{private} + (T - G) = I + NX$. It is an accounting identity: true every year in every country. It says the trade balance cannot change unless saving, investment or the government's budget balance changes too. Economists broadly agree on the identity; how saving and investment respond to policy is where they differ.

blocks.q: The government's deficit grows by \$200 billion, and private saving and investment stay the same. What happens to NX?
steps: $(T - G)$ falls by 200, so $NX$ must fall by 200.
In practice saving and investment also respond, so the trade balance need not move one-for-one; but something in the identity must give.
